cards.title: Simulation or postselection universality for two-qubit interactions
cards.formal: Does every fixed two-qubit Hamiltonian \(H\) satisfy the following dichotomy in the source’s circuit model: its computations are efficiently classically simulable, or they are universal for quantum computation under postselection? The system starts in a computational-basis state, uses only chosen-time applications of H or its inverse on ordered pairs of qubits, and is measured in the computational basis. H need not be commuting. The second branch was lost in the saved extraction; the general easy-branch accuracy and real-parameter conventions still need specification.
cards.why: Seeks a boundary between classically manageable quantum dynamics and postselection universality using only one fixed two-qubit interaction. The restriction to basis preparation and measurement makes computational power depend on more than ordinary unitary controllability.
cards.status_note: Read the full conference model, simulation definition and two-page question, checked the author’s 2017 thesis and arXiv version history, and checked the later analog-simulation theorem’s scope. Searches through 12 September 2026 found no general resolution. The remaining conventions prevent this draft from being certified as one fully specified open proposition.

Its precise commuting hardness theorem uses pointwise multiplicative error c<√2, which does not fix the easy-branch convention for arbitrary H. In addition, the source quantifies over arbitrary fixed Hermitian H and polynomial-bit time descriptions without a general representation/precision convention for their real constants. A completed benchmark must fix these conventions while preserving the basis-input, restricted-gate and postselection model; this review does not choose a new dichotomy on the source’s behalf.

sentences: The proposed dichotomy covers every fixed two-qubit interaction, including noncommuting ones.
Circuits begin and end in the computational basis and have no freely supplied local gates.
The alternatives are efficient classical simulation or universality under postselection.
The source handles commuting interactions, while later analog Hamiltonian-universality results use a different model.
The general easy-branch accuracy and numerical representation still need specification before the statement is complete.

cards.definitions:
A two-qubit Hamiltonian is a 4×4 Hermitian complex matrix H, fixed for an entire computational model rather than supplied as a growing input. A circuit may use polynomially many qubits, including ancillas initialized to known basis bits, and a polynomial-length sequence of gates \(e^{itH_{ij}}\), where i≠j is an ordered pair and t is a chosen real evolution time. Reversing the order of the pair applies the swapped interaction THT, with T exchanging |01⟩ and |10⟩. Negative times, equivalently exact access to −H, are allowed by the source. Other one-qubit gates, arbitrary local basis changes, arbitrary input states and intermediate adaptive measurements are not supplied for free.

A classical polynomial-time procedure, on the input bit string x, specifies the number of qubits, the basis input, the ordered sequence of pair applications and the time descriptions. The source requires polynomially many description bits and polynomially bounded time magnitudes. Since arbitrary H may not commute on overlapping pairs, the order and repetitions are part of a general circuit's description; the commuting special case may combine applications. Measuring all qubits in the computational basis yields a joint distribution P_x on bit strings. Constants in a putative simulation may depend on fixed H, but not arbitrarily on the input length.

Weak classical simulation means producing samples. For the source's precise multiplicative notion, a classical output distribution Q_x must satisfy \(P_x(z)/c\le Q_x(z)\le cP_x(z)\) for every x and output z. In particular, a zero-probability output must remain impossible. This differs from additive total-variation approximation, which bounds \(\frac12\sum_z|P_x(z)-Q_x(z)|\), and from strong simulation, which computes individual probabilities. Definition 2.2 and Theorem 2.3 specify a multiplicative hardness conclusion for commuting interactions; the general conjecture does not explicitly assign an accuracy quantifier or exact-sampling convention to its easy branch.

Postselection conditions the output on a specified nonzero-probability pattern of measurement outcomes, even if it occurs extremely rarely. It is not implemented by running the experiment until that event happens and charging that waiting time as polynomial. For language computation, the source specifies a designated decision bit and requires its conditional probability of being 1 to be at least 2/3 on yes inputs and at most 1/3 on no inputs. The postselection pattern is chosen uniformly in polynomial time; Definition 2.4 chooses it from the input length. Universality here means the ability to implement general postselected quantum computation with polynomial overhead, not just to produce one distribution with evidence of classical hardness.

A commuting H means that its copies on every pair commute, including opposite orientations and overlapping pairs. Equivalently the source requires [H⊗I,I⊗H]=[H⊗I,I⊗THT]=[H,THT]=0, with [A,B]=AB−BA. Its proved sampling dichotomy assumes this property. The general question removes it and allows computation on larger registers and encoded subspaces, so classifying which interactions generate every unitary on exactly two qubits is insufficient.

For a complete finite-computation statement, real constants in H and allowed evolution times need a representation and precision convention that supports uniform circuit generation and the selected simulator. The source's polynomial-bit wording alone does not specify that convention for arbitrary real H, especially in conjunction with exact or multiplicative simulation and rare postselection. This remains a formulation issue here, not a claimed negative solution based on noncomputable constants.
cards.answer_criterion: After fixing the stated simulation-accuracy and numerical conventions, prove that every permitted fixed H has at least one of the two properties, or exhibit an H for which both fail, stating any assumptions. Generic universality, a classification only of commuting H, hardness of some output probabilities, or universality with free local gates does not settle the general dichotomy. The polynomial-hierarchy-collapse consequence of suitable postselection universality is conditional; it is not an unconditional classical lower bound.

context_blocks.title: The missing half changes the question
context_blocks.text: The source asks for classical simulability or universality under postselection for every two-qubit interaction. The saved statement ended before the second alternative and obscured that the commuting case is already treated in the paper.

context_blocks.title: A proved special case
context_blocks.text: For commuting H, the paper proves that interactions generating entanglement from a computational-basis input cannot be weakly sampled with pointwise multiplicative error c<√2 unless the polynomial hierarchy collapses to its third level. Interactions that never generate such entanglement are described as simulable. This does not classify all noncommuting H.

context_blocks.title: The author’s thesis retains the general question
context_blocks.text: The September 2017 thesis repeats the conjecture in Section 4.8 and distinguishes larger-register and encoded computational universality from controllability on two qubits.

context_blocks.title: Analog universality is a different classification
context_blocks.text: The 2022 theorem relates universal analog Hamiltonian simulation to QMA-completeness under faithful reductions and closure of a Hamiltonian family. Those low-energy simulation conditions do not supply the basis-input sampling or postselection dichotomy for one fixed interaction.

cards.context:
The source asks for classical simulability or universality under postselection for every two-qubit interaction. The saved statement ended before the second alternative and obscured that the commuting case is already treated in the paper.

For commuting H, the paper proves that interactions generating entanglement from a computational-basis input cannot be weakly sampled with pointwise multiplicative error c<√2 unless the polynomial hierarchy collapses to its third level. Interactions that never generate such entanglement are described as simulable. This does not classify all noncommuting H.

The September 2017 thesis repeats the conjecture in Section 4.8 and distinguishes larger-register and encoded computational universality from controllability on two qubits.

The 2022 theorem relates universal analog Hamiltonian simulation to QMA-completeness under faithful reductions and closure of a Hamiltonian family. Those low-energy simulation conditions do not supply the basis-input sampling or postselection dichotomy for one fixed interaction.

methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. Our primary goal is a benchmark of 500 problems. Top 100 is a priority subset of those same 500, with secondary editorial attention. Both use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The existing Top 1000 view is not an active benchmark goal. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The legacy Top 1000 view has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The primary target is 500 problems; Top 100 is its priority subset with secondary editorial attention. Top 100, Top 500 and the legacy Top 1000 view use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.
